title: Principle and foundation
hookLine: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God; use things as far as they help

lines: A SOLDIER WITH A BROKEN LEG.
cards: A Basque soldier is carried home with a shattered leg. Stuck in bed for a long recovery, he asks for adventure stories. The house doesn't have any.
What it has is a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives. He reads them, out of boredom, and something in him turns. That's how his own Autobiography tells it.

His name is Ignatius of Loyola, and you first met him on day eight hundred seventy-three. Out of what happened next came a small handbook for a guide leading someone through prayer: the Spiritual Exercises.
A new room today, the Ignatian way, and it starts with one short paragraph the whole handbook stands on.

teach.b: Here's the paragraph, in plain words. Human beings are created to praise, reverence and serve God our Lord, and so to save their souls.
Everything else on the face of the earth is created for us, to help us toward that end.

teach.h: USE THINGS AS FAR AS THEY HELP.
teach.b: So we should use things as far as they help us toward it, and let go of them as far as they get in the way. It sounds dry, almost like an engineer wrote it. But it doesn't sort the world into holy things and bad things.
Money, a job, a phone, a friendship, an ambition: none of it is the enemy, and none of it is the point. Each one gets the same quiet question: does it help? The measure is the purpose, not the thing.
Paul had asked a similar question about Christian freedom: "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient." His Greek word for expedient, sympherei, means it's useful, it helps.
Plenty is allowed; not all of it helps. And the opening line matters as much as the rule.
Ignatius starts with what we're for: praise, reverence, service.
Revelation gives that note to the elders around God's throne: "Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things."
Begin there, in Ignatius's way of seeing, and every choice gets simpler, if not always easier: not what do I want, but what helps?

how: Jesuits and others who make the Spiritual Exercises, in a long retreat or in daily life with a guide, usually begin by praying with the Principle and Foundation, and return to it when making decisions.

o: Ignatius's base: we're made for God; use what helps
the first rule of the Jesuit order's daily life
a list of beliefs every Catholic must sign

p: created to help us toward it
use things as far as they help

s: the principle and foundation sorts the world into holy and bad things
it asks the same question of everything: does it help toward what we're made for?
Ignatius turned toward God while recovering from a battle wound
stuck in bed with a shattered leg, he read a life of Christ and the saints.
Paul says everything allowed is also helpful
all things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient.

games.q: you're making the Exercises. a new job offer comes, with more money and less time for the people you love. what's Ignatius's first question?
o: which option helps toward what I'm made for?
games.why: the principle and foundation measures every choice by the purpose: praise, reverence and service of God. use things as far as they help.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that takes up real space in your life, an app, a habit, a possession, and without judging it yet, hold it up and ask: does this help me toward what I'm for?
If you pray, you can ask God to show you; if you don't, ask whether it helps you love and serve well. Notice the answer, even if it's mixed.

wordCard.voice: Principle and foundation. The opening of Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises: we're made to praise, reverence and serve God, and we use everything else as far as it helps.

orig.note: Greek: it is useful, it helps; the word the King James renders expedient in 1 Corinthians 6:12.

carryVoice: Your line: as far as it helps. Not good or bad, just: does it help? Until tomorrow.
